utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Today, Judge Mindua being absent, Judge Harhoff and I sit pursuant to the provisions of Rule 15 bis, and Mr. Tapuskovic, you were to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I still have a few things that I needed to clarify with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you know that last time there was talk about the transcript from the Galic case, about the home for the blind and about the way the transcript was interpreted by my learned friend, the Prosecutor, Mr. Sachdeva. So I would like to have it shown on the ELMO -- actually, page 14224, line 22, and page 14225, until line 6 -- up to line 6, so that the interpreters can translate to the witness what he said so that I could ask him questions about that because my learned friend, the Prosecutor, put some things to the witness in a way that did not or does not accord with the transcript in relation to the home for the blind. That would be that page. It's line 22. So could the interpreters please translate what it says in those lines? There is no translation. I can't hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are we having the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard the translation, the complete translation, into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Only the B/C/S booth was working. We were interpreting what the translation is on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there was talk about him saying earlier that he was once in the home for the blind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that, Witness? If you heard the translation, is it true that you spoke about showing the intersection between Bosna Srebena and Lukavica street and that to the question if you were in any of those buildings, did you go to any of these buildings between September 1992 and August 1994, any of those buildings? Isn't it correct you were asked if you visited or went to any of the buildings, but not about you going actually to the home of the blind -- for the blind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, any building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And that once -- and that you were in one of those buildings with your commander at one point in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So there was no mention of you being in the building that housed the home for the blind; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show the witness Prosecution Exhibit P783? Can we zoom on the document, please? Thank you. And now, could the usher please assist the witness and give him a different coloured marker? A colour other than blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please first point to where the Gusica Hala was here that you talked about before? Can you please mark that with a letter G?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you draw a line between that place and the place where the home of the blind was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark that with the letter S, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The location, as you -- that you marked as Gusica Hala and that you discussed last time, where you were almost hit, that was your position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not during the entire war. I can indicate the position where I was for most of the war period. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark that with the letter R?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now, I would like you to mark with a red line on either side, in order to get out of this area, where you had to go.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm wondering how this arises out of cross-examination. Perhaps I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you only wondering?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I submit that does not arise out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Tapuskovic, what aspect of the cross-examination does this relate to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, this map, this map, all of this, was indicated at the request of the Prosecution, marked at the request of the Prosecution, and now, in order to understand this, we need to get from the witness additional explanations. Here is the first thing that would be important. From which directions was there firing on this area that is marked in this way by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before that, of course, you need to decide whether the objection is justified because this map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic, for allowing me to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, we are not with you on this one. We believe that it does arise. So the questioning may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, Witness, can you please indicate on this map where Mojmilo is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about Mojmilo hill?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. You cannot see the top of the hill, but it lies from this name here, Mojmilo, that is the Mojmilo settlement, and then it goes on and you cannot see where it ends.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where is Stup, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. Well, it's the broader area, wider area of the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you indicate the direction from which firing came to this area where you lived and can you please indicate this with appropriate arrows, pointing in the right direction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you mark that arrow with the letter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise and with great respect, I know you have ruled, but I simply asked the witness to mark certain locations in Nedzarici, because that was his AOR. I did not ask the witness questions about the origin of fire from the ABiH. In fact, Mr. Tapuskovic himself led that evidence in his examination-in-chief. And so in my submission, going back to that subject which is now what the Defence counsel appears to be doing, with these later questions, my submission is that they really do not arise out of cross-examination. I have no problem if the witness is asked to mark certain other locations within Nedzarici or to explain the markings that he has made in cross-examination but now to move on to firing from Stup and Mojmilo when that had been touched upon already -- or not just touched upon but had been dealt with in the examination-in-chief, in my submission, it is -- it's redundant now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the Prosecutor has more specifically explained why your question does not arise out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm going to explain. I'm going to ask him. You see here Alipasino Polje and there was a lot of talk about what you can see from the whole -- home of the blind in that direction, where a boy was shot, a young man, and it was insisted that the army of Republika Srpska was firing from these buildings that were facing Alipasino Polje. The Prosecutor insisted that firing came from this area. But I think that it's very important to know that precisely from those locations, and Alipasino Polje, there was intense firing on these positions on which the Prosecutor insisted. So then the next thing that I would ask the witness to tell us would be if there was firing from this direction of Alipasino Polje on the positions indicated here by the Prosecutor as the places from where there was intensive firing upon the positions of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, tell us exactly what you're leading to. Where is this re-examination leading? What is the conclusion that you hope to arrive at?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the assistance of this situation that has been marked on the request of the Prosecutor, and with the assistance of the next photograph that will be shown, my interest, which needs to be explained to you and which is important, is that from these lines here, in view of this entire situation that is here surrounded by hills and the tall buildings on Alipasino Polje, the only firing possible was from the cellars of all those buildings and even from the home for the blind. So these were houses, very -- not very high, perhaps two storeys at the most, surrounded by high buildings, which I'm going to show on the following photograph, indicating that any kind of firing from an elevated position would have been ruled out in view of the situation in which this line here where the home of the blind is located towards Alipasino Polje and towards Mojmilo and this will then later be linked with the photograph which is Prosecutor Exhibit P100, in order for us to be able to understand all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva? You wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, my submission is this: If Mr. Tapuskovic had put a question to the witness asking him whether the only possible position to fire from would have been the cellars, that would have been objectionable in terms of it being leading and now, Mr. Tapuskovic has explained the thesis or explained what he thinks to be the evidence, and my submission is that the witness therefore cannot give -- or his answer is likely to be prejudiced, in my submission. In other words, it has the same effect of asking leading questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But counsel was really answering the question that I -- that I asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may ask the question, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you mark with an arrow the direction fired from upon the line you've indicated, including the home for the blind, by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about Mojmilo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. I cannot indicate that on the map but as for Mojmilo hill --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think this is enough. I'd like to tender this as Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D260, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I cannot mark on this map where the fire came from the direction of Igman, since we cannot see Mount Igman here. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You're trying to tell us that they also acted from that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They used various artillery pieces. For a while they also had a launcher, an improvised one. They used certain contraptions and it had a lot of explosive power until the device itself exploded somewhere on Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This was a spontaneous answer by the witness but I believe it to be important nonetheless. Perhaps we should tender this map anew since he had entered some new markings on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D261, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a look at the photograph I mentioned? It is Prosecution Exhibit P100. I would kindly ask the usher to provide another pen to the witness of a different colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you circle the buildings in this photograph from which there was firing against the positions held by you, first and foremost having in mind the building marked with an S?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. I think one should mark the entire complex in the background, the one that we can't see entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Behind the building marked with an S and the circles that we can see in the corners shown to you yesterday, across the line which separates the photograph into two parts, were there any buildings from which one could open fire upon you as well as in some other directions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you indicate those?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These buildings here, this area. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark the area with the letter M?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Put an H in the biggest circle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the right-hand side area should be marked with a G.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is the name of the settlement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-48 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alipasino Polje and Vjnicko Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your evidence. Mr. Sachdeva were you trying to rise?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm minded not to, although I wonder whether I would be permitted to ask some questions of the witness, since again in my submission, this could have been put to the witness in the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I forgot. This photograph should be tendered as a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let it be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D262, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, I think not, because the Chamber had ruled that the questions did arise. Witness, this concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, and I thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next witness will not require much time. It is Witness T-5. And he enjoys certain protective measures, this being a pseudonym and image distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please be seated. You may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to introduce this witness to the Court, we shall have to make use of document DD00388.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: D003989.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to tender this document under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D263, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we move into private session for a while?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have been allocated a very short period of time for your examination and I would kindly ask you to be as brief as possible. When the events began evolving in Sarajevo in 1992, where were you and what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-5
utterances.text: I used to live in Nedzarici until 1992. I stayed there until the 18th of May 1992, until I saw people being killed and houses being set on fire. I moved out of there, together with my child. We moved to Kasindol.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-5
utterances.text: To the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where is the hospital in Kasindol and how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-5
utterances.text: The Kasindol hospital is about three to four kilometres away from Nedzarici itself. I think it's about three to four kilometres. I'm not particularly certain of that. We were received there as refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many days did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-5
utterances.text: I stayed there for 10 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you go next, briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-5
utterances.text: From there, I went to Grbavica in Sarajevo. Grbavica was a part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about Kasindol? Where was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-5
utterances.text: Kasindol is also in Sarajevo. Bratska [phoen] municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you stay for the rest of the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-5
utterances.text: I stayed in Grbavica throughout the war until the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please describe, in the briefest possible way, what life was like in Grbavica? How did you live in Grbavica at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-5
utterances.text: I was in basements throughout that period in Grbavica, together with other residents who were there in that building. There were Muslims, Croats and Serbs there, all those who lived there before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you go just a little bit faster? Just a little bit faster. And can you describe what life was like initially and what were you able to notice? If you were in the basement, were you able to see anything from there or hear anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-5
utterances.text: We were in basements or cellars because of safety, because you could hear shooting all day long in Grbavica. We spent the whole time there. We had a radio, although there was no electricity. It was a battery-operated radio. We listened to reports every day, what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. And can you please tell me how you lived, in terms of just ordinary activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-5
utterances.text: We spent the whole day in the basement, and at night we would supply ourselves with food and water and we were able to go out during the night. During the day, we didn't dare to because there was shooting, constant shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what did you find out from listening to the radio?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Objection. Two objections, Mr. President. Number 1, to relevancy. I've hesitated to rise on a question of relevancy because the witness has obviously been through a very difficult time, but we have a witness here who has all but disqualified herself as a witness by saying that she spent any time that she would have had an opportunity to observe relevant events in a basement, unable to see, and I also put it, again I understand of course that hearsay evidence is admissible but if the question is what the witness heard on the radio, there are far better sources of transcripts of news programmes available than relying on the years past memory of a witness, and I respectfully put it to the Chamber that particularly in a situation where better and more reliable evidence is available, that evidence such as this should not be admitted and I again stress I do not rise on a point of hearsay because I understand that that is admissible. I rise on a point of reliability. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will hear what the witness has to say but I'd like Mr. Tapuskovic, at all times, to extract from the witness the basis of her knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you're absolutely right, and I did make a mistake. In fact, she mentioned the radio. What I wanted to ask her first, however, was that if she was able to notice anything by herself from the basement throughout that period. This is what I wanted to ask her about. But then she mentioned the radio, and I wanted to expand on that but, of course, I would like to ask the witness first what she herself was able to see, and was she able to see anything of the events at Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Lay the foundation for the witness's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, you said that throughout that time period, and we'll see whether it was the entire period or later, that you spent that in the basement. Were you able to -- was it possible to see anything of what was going on outside from the basement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-5
utterances.text: The basement where we were had small windows through which you could see everything that was going on in the street. Every day I would watch civilians getting killed on the streets, and we were helpless to assist them because we were also exposed to danger. I personally saw when a boy was hit. His mother went up to him to help. The mother was also hit. And they remained there on the street until it got dark. No one was able to help them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell me if, at any point, there was a time when such things were not so frequent?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, whether they are frequent or not, would you explain the relevance of this evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, this is the continuation of what we were talking about. It's an incident this she remembers very well and I intend to ask her further how often such things happened and if after that, during those war years, there was ever a period when it was easier, and that is why I believe that what is important, in terms of this witness, is for the witness first to describe what they were able to see and that we get from her testimony the terror that they were subjected to, also the problem related to the campaign that is referred to in the indictment, and whether at some stage what the Prosecution calls here a campaign could have been eliminated and for her actually to talk about things that relate to the essence of the indictment, especially during the period relating to General Milosevic. What she's talking about is up to some certain period and then later there was a different situation and then all of these things that had to do with this campaign and that are related to the terror that they were subjected to, the dangers that their children were exposed to, and everything that the civilians were subjected to, all this in Sarajevo itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is not clear to me is that if one agrees that they did suffer terror, that they were exposed to terror, how is that relevant to the indictment which charges the accused with inflicting, through his troops, a campaign of terror on civilians? How do you answer that charge by adducing evidence that this witness and her neighbours did, in fact, experience terror themselves? We are back to the theme of Serb suffering.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I never put in question at any point in time anybody's suffering. What I wish to show is that the time period of the indictment was completely different, and that there was no campaign at that time in relation to anyone, not in relation to civilians either, and that that time, at the end of a period that refers to General Milosevic, some things occurred that had nothing to do with the intention of the army of Republika Srpska to cause suffering in any way for anyone, and that that was -- there was a long period where there was no such campaign, and when the army of Republika Srpska did not ever have, as its cause, especially not things that relate to General Milosevic, not in any of the neighbourhoods, Nedzarici, Dobrinja and others in this broader period which all these areas that constitute the area of Sarajevo, all of this which was a product of permanent conflicts which were considerably reduced at the time and there was absolutely nothing that could have been described as a campaign so that all of that together, directly disputes the things that are cited in the indictment, if we view that further in the context of the positions that were occupied at the time. In any case, I think that this witness, in view of what she went through, would be able to tell us something to the effect that, for a considerable period of time, it was possible to go out into the street, that there was no such campaign, and to show you in that way that the indictment, the way it is formulated in relation to the time period in which the responsibility is ascribed to the accused, Dragomir Milosevic, is something that had absolutely not the qualification of a campaign, which occupies a central point in the indictment, as an action that is dominating in the whole of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all respect to my learned friend Mr. Tapuskovic, I think if this witness had been inside the confrontation line and said that for a while, for periods of time, there was no terror that might be relevant evidence. I stress might. Here we have a witness though who was in Grbavica on the Bosnian Serb side of the confrontation lines in a basement observing things through a window and cannot speak about what was going on with civilians inside the confrontation lines and therefore, I renew the relevancy objection I made sometime ago and that the court on its own initiative raised with respect to the pending question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He insists that the witness will give evidence to the effect that there was no campaign of terror. What isn't clear to me is how he intends to achieve that because the witness is merely giving evidence of terror that she suffered. This is -- we have been through this before but I still don't quite grasp it, Mr. Tapuskovic. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague, Mr. Docherty, has just stated what is being accentuated all the time. Inside of what? This witness was inside this concept of inside. So that is an area that could not have been separated from that concept which is being constantly defined as "inside" or "within." She was inside and within. So I specifically wanted to hear why she was in the basement for a long, long time and then to explain when this stopped for a little bit and how life was at that time, and then to specifically testify about what she saw and directly experienced and how, during those war years, there was a phase during which it was possible to breathe and live, and that is something that is important. So the witness is going to come. I wasn't able be to--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why is it important? We are not interested in whether there was a time in which it was possible to breathe and live. We are not writing a history of the Sarajevo conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would have to open the indictment. What dominates in the indictment is a campaign of activities against civilians and civilian facilities. That is the main count of the indictment. This terror based on a permanent campaign to exclusively fire on civilians and the civilian population, and that that campaign, as I said last time, had it not been explained, Your Honours, countless times and probably I'll have to do it again and last time I already talked about that, that the Prosecution, a month before the indictment period begins, had they not changed the indictment and set out from the untenable position that Dragomir Milosevic inherited the campaign from Galic, that he took over and continued with it, believe me, I wouldn't have mentioned 1991 or 1992 or 1993 or a large amount of 1994, and I would have started from the 12th of August 1994, two days after that the agreement was signed which alleviated the situation for a few months. I would have dealt with that. And as Defence counsel representing Dragomir Milosevic, I would have been in a much easier position. After the Prosecution amended the indictment, stating that Dragomir Milosevic inherited this campaign, I had to deal with that problem. I already talked about that several times, how that looked in those previous few years and after, how that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, the amendment admittedly does let in some evidence from 1991-1992. But the evidence still has to relate to the indictment. And that's what is not at all clear to me. It seems to be just evidence about her suffering and, of course, we are very sorry for that, and I'd like to assure her that she has our full sympathy. But we don't find this evidence relevant, Mr. Tapuskovic. So move on to another area and see whether you can extract from this witness evidence that is relevant to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It means that each and every time I will have to deal with this issue of inheriting the campaign. If I do away with it, it will make my job far easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Chamber what the end of 1994 was like, what was your life like at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-5
utterances.text: By the end of 1994, things got much calmer. We could move about. We went out. We were much more free to move, until June 1995, when, in Grbavica, there was so much firing taking place there that we had no idea what was happening. That was the most difficult period, which lasted until the Dayton Accords were signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since you said that, I would kindly ask you to -- and after that, I'll conclude shortly. Could you please tell us, since you lived under the circumstances you described, meaning you could go out in the street and move more freely; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-5
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What could you hear over the radio at that time, before that and at that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-5
utterances.text: Over the radio, we listened to the Muslim media non-stop. They boasted of killing numbers or scores of Serbian soldiers and they never mentioned civilians, whereas they described the situation on their side completely the opposite. They said that only civilians were being killed, whereas not a single soldier was lost on their part. We felt that this was adding insult to injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I renew the relevancy objection previously made. The witness -- I can't stress enough the witness has my full sympathy and I don't like to get up in a courtroom and quickly say that what she has to say is not relevant but unfortunately it is not relevant. If the witness has something to say about what was going on in the area under the command of the ABiH, the area where civilians were being terrorised, the Prosecution submits, by troops under the command of the accused, I would certainly have no relevancy objection to that but we continue simply to hear of what is going on outside the confrontation lines in SKR-controlled territory and I submit that it simply is not relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We agree it's not relevant, Mr. Tapuskovic. It may very well be that the witness has no evidence to give that's relevant. And I would very much regret that because she has been brought here. But if that is the case, then, let us reach that point very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the reason for this witness being here was stated by the witness herself. She said that as of the fall of 1994, until summer 1995, they lived in a normal way. She didn't say that during that period she felt threatened in any way, that her life was in danger, and this is what is directly relevant to the indictment. She also stated that after that, there was mayhem and horror as described by her. And that horror was created because of the activities of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The witness may not know that but it was caused by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is our case. For a full eight months, when things went as normal, and then there was chaos. It is Defence's position that this chaos was caused by an all-out offensive by the ABiH. This lady is here to confirm to that you life went on as usual for almost eight months. She confirmed that. This should be weighed ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, the campaign alleged by the indictment, was it confined to the area covered by the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Give me a moment, Your Honour, and I'll get the exact language from the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, perhaps you can address that matter as well, since it is important to the question that we are now considering.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will not refer to each and every paragraph, but if we start with paragraph 5 and then go through all the rest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Paragraph 5. Let us look at them individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 5, it says under the effective control of Dragomir Milosevic conducted a campaign of sniping and shelling against the civilian population of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What the Prosecutor is saying is that for the evidence to be relevant, it must relate to the area covered by the confrontation line. That may be an overly narrow view, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, I really don't think so. The indictment read in a commonsensical manner and as a whole clearly indicates that the defendant -- or the accused, excuse me, perpetrated a campaign of terror against, it does say civilian areas of Sarajevo. Every single scheduled incident put forth in this indictment relates to areas inside the confrontation line. It is no way a defence to the charge of terror or any other charge in the indictment to show that people in -- outside the confrontation lines had lulls during which they could go about their daily business and I would also point out that the lull that has been testified to by this witness is a so-called lull that relates to -- that -- in which a large number of the Prosecution's scheduled incidents occurred. To say that, well, there was not fighting in this particular area for a while and it's an area that was under the command of the SRK in the first place is really no defence and as I say, an indictment ought not to be parsed out line by line. It ought to be read as a whole which is the way it's written which is the way it gives notice to the accused of the charges he has to meet, and this indictment clearly alleges a campaign of terror against civilians in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, the -- you heard that. The point he's making is that when you read the indictment as a whole, his submission is that the campaign relates to the confrontation lines, civilians living within the confrontation lines. Would you care to point us to other paragraphs which support the position that you're taking?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, look, for example, at counts 5 to 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That's what I was just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Conducted a campaign, in the fourth line, of artillery and mortar and modified air bomb shelling on to civilian areas of Sarajevo and upon its civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is no geographical demarcation there. The only one is to Sarajevo. But I imagine you would answer that by saying that when you look at the context in which the case arises, when you look at the case as a whole, the campaign was confined to the confrontation lines. The thinking that I'm developing is along these lines, that Mr. Tapuskovic is saying that the lull in the fighting in the area where this witness lived, albeit some distance from the confrontation lines, assists in contradicting the Prosecution's case that there was a campaign, which has an element of continuity. No. I -- Let me just finish the thought that I'm having, which is that the evidence may be admissible. At the end of the day, at the end of the case, the Chamber will have to determine what weight it attaches to it. It may say this deserves very little or no weight but I don't know whether that your point is sufficient to warrant its exclusion, to say that it is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. While the Court was consulting I was looking by coincidence at the very same language, and I draw attention, with respect, to the way in which this campaign was said to be carried out, beginning again with the 4th line conducted a campaign -- or excuse me, Bosnian Serb forces comprising or attached to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and/or forces affiliated with the VRS conducted a campaign of artillery and mortar and modified air bomb shelling on to civilian areas of Sarajevo and upon its civilian population. Unless we are going to go down the road of the SRK was shelling areas under its own command and sniping them and air bombing them, there is, I respectfully submit, no interpretation of this indictment other than that the SRK was sniping and mortaring and artillery firing and modified air bomb launching on to areas not under its control. And if we look at the top of this same page, there is a carry-over from the previous page, again talking about the civilian population of Sarajevo, killing and wounding a large number of them, and then the last line, before the -- the last line of that carry-over paragraph specific instances of these attacks include by way of illustrative allegations those incidents set forth in the first schedule to this indictment and there is similar language at the end of the 5 to 7 shelling counts. The illustrative allegations, the scheduled incidents, all occur within the confrontation lines. The campaign is alleged to be carried out by sniping and shelling and launching air bombs by the SRK or forces affiliated with the SRK. And I -- to bring a witness who says, well, but on territory under the control of the SRK things were fine from time to time, does not contradict the evidence of the Prosecution witnesses who have testified in this trial that they were on trams and were shot during this lull, that air bombs landed in among other places, Hrasnica, during this lull. The witness has talked about, I believe, the fall of 1995 as being the end of the lull so this includes the launching the air bomb on to the television tower occurring during this lull. Things were probably indeed better outside the confrontation lines but I respectfully submit that that is not relevant to meeting the case that the Prosecution has put forward. And then my last point would be that at no time during our Prosecution case comprising some months did we lead evidence concerning SRK attacks on SRK-controlled positions, and the indictment, I respectfully submit, does need to be interpreted in light of the case, in the context of the case, that the Prosecution has put forward. Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's a difficult issue. The Chamber, however, concludes that the evidence is not relevant, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please allow me to respond to what my learned friend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I don't want a response. We have had several arguments from the -- from you. I've heard you at least twice and I've heard the Prosecutor the same number of times. And we have ruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honours. I will not question the witness further. But please, I must respond to what Mr. Docherty has said, in order to deal with what we will soon hear from other witnesses. I must respond to what Mr. Docherty has just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. We have -- I have ruled and we should move on. If you have other arguments which may arise in relation to the evidence of other witnesses, then you can bring those arguments at that time, during their testimony. But we've heard both sides on this issue. I'm satisfied that I have given you a hearing on this question, and I've given the Prosecutor a hearing, and I've given my ruling. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course there is nothing I can do, Your Honours, in this situation, but I have not been given an opportunity to raise two or three important points in relation to what the Prosecutor has said about the confrontation line. I have not had the opportunity to explain this in order for this witness's evidence to be understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we have heard from you, and we have heard enough on this issue to enable us to come to a decision, and we have given that decision. Do you have any other evidence from this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge at all about where Grbavica was fired at from? As regards its geographical location, where were the hills? And did you know what the situation in Grbavica was like and who was where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-5
utterances.text: It was mostly from Mojmilo and Debelo Brdo and Loris that shots were fired at Grbavica. From Loris there was a sniper firing all the time. I lived in that area and we couldn't even peep out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what is Loris?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-5
utterances.text: I heard that on television and the radio that that was where most of the shots were fired from, from Loris, and this was held by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS T-5
utterances.text: They boasted on the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have no cross-examination for this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take a break, a break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Be seated. And you may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, before you begin answering my questions, I would like to tell you that we should both bear in mind that you should begin answering only when the text you see appearing on the monitor before you stops. Witness, can you tell Their Honours your first and last name?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: My name is Radomir Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were born on the 11th of May 1942. Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were born in the town of Olovo near Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You completed primary school in Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please wait for the text on the monitor to stop before answering. You completed your secondary school for economics and the first two years of the faculty of economics in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you have been living in Sarajevo since 1962 in your family house at Vrace overlooking Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You worked in the factory called Zrak in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, could you tell Their Honours the following? Like every citizen of the former federal -- Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, you served in the JNA. Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. All able-bodied men who had a university education, were sent to a reserve officers school, and we attended a course which lasted for 12 months, and then we became reserve second lieutenants. After that, when there were exercises, military exercises, we would be called to participate and then we might be promoted to the rank of Lieutenant or captain and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you serve in the army of that former country?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: From 1968, from late March 1968, to 1969, sometime around the 17th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You remember the dates. And after that, did you have anything to do with the JNA apart from the obligatory exercises that all citizens had to participate in from time to time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when in that system that we lived in, the communist system prevailing at the time, the so-called Territorial Defence was established?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was established after the so-called constitution of 1974 when the republics of Yugoslavia were granted more or less the same rights as states, and each country -- or rather each republic had its own territorial forces which had certain weapons, which they -- of which they were the owners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where were these weapons kept from 1974 onwards?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you precisely all the places where these weapons were kept, but as far as I know, those weapons were stored in various military districts such as the Sarajevo district, the Zenica district, the Tuzla, Banja Luka, Mostar districts, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Quite specifically, you lived at Vrace. Did you know where weapons were kept there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, to be specific, I lived at Vrace, but I did not know where the weapons were stored. I did learn later on that they were stored up there -- I can't remember the precise name of the place where the weapons were stored, but it was in the direction of Kosevo. I'm not sure however.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, in 1974, did you understand what these weapons were for, what purpose they served, their being stored among the people?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can recall, there were certain people, educated people, who, in a very discreet manner, criticised this fact. They thought that the republics had been given too much independence and they had weapons. As there was a single JNA, that was supposed to be the guarantee of our common state of Yugoslavia. However, this criticism was not taken into account, and what was done was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did you know what happened in 1991 and what these Territorial Defences turned into, starting from Slovenia all the way to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, what the critics had been saying since 1974 proved to be true, because the Slovenian territorials killed a certain number of members of the JNA which up to that point had been the joint army. In Slovenia there were Bosnian soldiers, Macedonian soldiers, Croatian soldiers, Serb soldiers, and on the other hand, in our parts, there were Slovenes, Macedonians, Montenegrins, Serbs and Croats serving in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So what did these Territorial Defences turn into in Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, they became armed forces which were subordinated to their own republican commands. The Slovenian to the Republic of Slovenia, the Croatian Territorial Defence to Tudjman, if I may say, as the President of Croatia. And in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it became divided into three parts because we had three constituent nations, Croats, Muslims and Serbs. The Croats and the Muslims were in one community and we Serbs were separate, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said the Croats and the Muslims were in a single community but did this last throughout the conflict?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: No. They acted together, jointly, until 1993, and I think that in 1993, conflicts broke out between the Croats and the Muslims, and I must tell Their Honours that at the Nis plateau, when the Muslims attacked the Croats from Breza, our forces pulled out a large number of Croats and sent them on towards Kiseljak and they were very grateful to us. But then they assisted some of our forces in Zenica and other parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let's move to the specific situation. Where were you employed from -- well, after completing your education? In which factory did you work?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: I worked in a factory called Zrak in Sarajevo. It produced civilian and military equipment. The civilian equipment we produced were glasses. We produced electrical equipment for military vehicles, and microscopes for laboratories, civilian laboratories. We also produced binoculars used for hunting. For the army we produced snipers and other equipment, according to the orders we received. For example, the JNA might order certain kinds of equipment and the contract would be drawn up and then it would be executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell Their Honours what work you did?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: I was in the commercial department. I was the chief of the department for the import of optical parts. I cooperated with a company in Delft. I -- or rather a company in Frankfurt, where I travelled often.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where was this factory?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: In a place called Buca Potok. If you look down from Vrace towards the hill of Hum on the left side of Hum there is a valley in which our factory was located, the factory of Zrak Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Until when were you able to go to work in Buca Potok?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: I was able to go to Buca Potok until around the 15th of May. That was my last day at work. After that, I was no longer able to go there because in the area around Buca Potok and below Hum in a place called Pofalici, on the 18th of May there was a fierce attack by the BH army, and 18 people were killed and 28 wounded. Our people, both civilians and soldiers. And after that, one could no longer reach Zrak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do then? How did you behave subsequently and what happened?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, when this started, the way it did, then we had to self-organise and we had to protect our homes, our families, so that on the right side, towards the Jewish cemetery, we set up our own defence lines and then down towards the Miljacka river, practically to the Vrbanja bridge, all the way to the Bratstvo-Jedinstvo street.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: That's the Grbavica part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when General Dragomir Milosevic became the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Milosevic, according to what I know, came in August. I think it was in mid-August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell me, if you know, when approximately the Yugoslav People's Army left the area around Sarajevo, and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: The evacuation and the departure of the JNA units from Sarajevo was done according to the last deadline, that was the 20th of May. That's when the Yugoslav People's Army left the centre area and the part where the main command of General Kukanjac was. This was in Bistrik street. They also left the other barracks in the direction of Nedzarici. So they all left by the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened with the soldiers who were leaving that area in that period? You can just give us a few indications about that.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you the truth, Your Honours, that on the 2nd and the 3rd of May, there was a massacre that was committed. This is all well known. This was done by the paramilitary or actual military forces in Skenderija, when innocent officers, non-commissioned officers, doctors, nurses, medical technicians were killed. 42 were killed, 75 were injured. These were all staff and 242 soldiers were captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we have been over this ground before. The information concerning events in 1992 has been held by the Chamber to be not relevant, with the limited exception of attempts at rebutting paragraph 7 of the indictment, and I submit that the evidence just led by Mr. Tapuskovic is, consistent with those earlier rulings, not relevant and not admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me just clarify. The Chamber has not ruled that evidence relating to 1992 is relevant. We are dealing with each case on its own merits. When an objection is made, we'll examine the objection and determine whether the evidence is relevant. We haven't made a ruling that applies to 1992 as a whole. So we'll now look at this objection that you have made. We'll hear from Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Docherty didn't wait for my next question, and it would then be easier for me to explain this for you but here I am again in the situation of needing to deal with this issue. The beginning of the conflict is something that is particularly emphasised in the indictment, the indictment insists on the Sarajevo locality and the indictment insists on a series of other things pertaining to the start of the conflict, without which there would be absolutely nothing in the area where for 40 years those three people lived together in harmony, and the beginning is covered by the indictment and we always have to go back to count 7, where very important things are discussed in relation to the position of those who took part in that conflict subsequently. This witness knows a lot about that and I think he explained very ably to you what the circumstances were that preceded the conflict and we have just now reached the situation which forced the people who lived there after the events at Pofalici and Buca Potok and after what the Yugoslav People's Army went through, to take up arms. He said earlier that he would have never have taken up arms usually but he was forced to stand and defend his home, his hearth, and he's going to tell you what his experiences are in relation to this and the beginnings which led to the tragic events are very important. They are covered by the indictment here in paragraph 7. It is very well put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Even it says that the conflict broke out in Sarajevo very quickly after the 7th of April 1992, when Bosnia and Herzegovina was internationally recognised. And then it says even before this date, armed forces supporting the Serbian Democratic Party and elements of the JNA including units of the 4th Corps occupied strategic positions in and around Sarajevo, the city was subsequently subjected to blockade and relentless bombardment and sniper attacks. Much of the bombardment and sniping was from positions in the hills around and overlooking Sarajevo from which the attackers had a clear detailed and commanding view of the city and its civilian population. This witness will specifically deal and explain -- deal with and explain what the situation was on the 7th of April, what the positions were that were taken up, and if we continue, you will see, as in count 8, on or around 20th -- 8th [as interpreted] 1992 and we just talked about that, after a partial withdrawal of JNA forces from Bosnia, and this witness explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow this evidence, but bring the witness to 1994 as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, and, in particular, this, the JNA practically transformed into part of the newly established army of Republika Srpska. So these are crucial positions of the Prosecution, and these are matters that I wish to question the witness about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, the place where you lived, how did you organise yourselves? In what way? Does the JNA have anything to do with whatever the place was where you were?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: No. They had nothing to do with that. We practically used our reserve officers and non-commissioned officers from the former JNA, and we received some weapons from the former JNA. In the beginning we had some hunting weapons, whoever happened to have something, and we created platoons and companies but this was still part of the TO, the Territorial Defence, brigades of the Novo Sarajevo municipality which started to operate. We put up the defence lines in order to stop them from killing our wives, our children and burning our property.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I interrupted the witness as he was saying that he stayed there in order to defend his house and his property. That wasn't entered in the transcript. If need be, the witness can repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We organised ourselves because that was a TO brigade of Novo Sarajevo municipality. We had platoons and companies that merged in order to protect the population that was in danger between the Jewish cemetery and the hill of Hum, as well as to the hill that was to my left. To my right, there was Debelo Brdo and to the left, well, I cannot recall the name, as well as towards the Miljacka. Grbavica is there. I described it already between the Jewish cemetery and the Vrbanja bridge all the way down to the brotherhood unity bridge and the stadium of Sdelznica. To my left towards Mojmilo and to my right was Debelo Brdo held by the forces of...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have to go back to the time for which you said that in the second part of August 1994, Dragomir Milosevic was appointed commander of the SRK. I have to show you a map. It is a 65 ter document 2872. Once you have the map before you, I'd like to ask to you explain or to show the positions at which you were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we zoom in, please? A bit more and down, downwards. No, sorry, up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before I ask you anything about the positions that you had occupied, can you please say when this Territorial Defence and your self-organising turned into activities of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps went into operation -- well, actually our TO belonged to the 1st Sarajevo Brigade -- in 1992. This was sometime in June, in early June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please indicate where your house is?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: My house is here. This is the Dervisa Numica [phoen] street now. Across from there was the Aleksa Bojevic cultural hall and immediately next to it was our infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you need to make the circle.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. That was here. My house was on that road. And to the left of that was the cultural hall and the infirmary or the medical station, and that was destroyed on the 10th of June. It was shelled from Mojmilo hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You need to wait for the question, Mr. Visnjic. Yes. Can you please explain -- okay, that's where your house was, and now you need to tell me when the lines of separation were formed between the VRS and the ABiH and can you please draw in these lines of separation on this map, from your positions?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: From my positions at Vrace and Grbavica, this is the area of Vrace where positions were held in this area, in the direction of Miljacka and then it goes there in the direction of the Jewish cemetery, where Debelo Brdo is, and here were the forces of the -- [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please don't rush, Mr. Visnjic. Just wait for the question.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where is Debelo Brdo or rather Mojmilo and can you please circle that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. Mojmilo is exactly in this area here, and that was under the control --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Take it slowly, please. Just indicate it.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is where Mojmilo was [Marks]. That was occupied by the B and H federation forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And what was the position of the hill in relation to the location of your house?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: That is elevation 680 or 690, as far as I know. So from Mojmilo they had an overview of the entire Vrace, to Grbavica, over the Zeljo Stadium, all the way down to the Miljacka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And which was Vrace elevation?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: The Vrace elevation was at some 480 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please mark the Mojmilo circle with the letter M?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please indicate where Debelo Brdo is? Can you please mark it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Debelo Brdo was to the right here. [Marks]. And I think that that was at an elevation of 750 metres. So it was higher. And it was the vantage point that would cover our entire right side, and this one would cover our left side from Mojmilo. So we were constantly under bursts of fire from the B and H army. From Debelo Brdo you can control the depth towards Miljevic and Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Mr. Visnjic, please don't hurry, just wait for my questions. When was this line of separation definitely set, the line of separation between the VRS and the ABiH? And when I say that, I mean in every respect.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: It was definitely established in July, the lines of Republika Srpska and the B and H army. During the war, they changed to a certain extent, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You talked about April and the pullout of the JNA. You said in July. What was the date and what does this refer to that this was definite on the 18th of July or whatever date you said? Did you say July or June?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, July. I think that Republika Srpska at the time headed by Radovan Karadzic, who was in charge --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let's leave Radovan Karadzic aside. What I'm asking you is when the definite lines were established. You indicated Mojmilo here and Debelo Brdo. Is there anything about Zlatiste?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: As far as Zlatiste that is something -- Zlatiste was our only road, the only way out from Grbavica towards Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, just one moment, please. I'm asking you when the army of Republika Srpska began also to control Zlatiste.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: As late as the 16th of July 1992, we managed to occupy Zlatiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have a look at the map and its western part. Or, rather, let us save this map as it is, as a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you asking for this to be an exhibit, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D264, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please have this map shown again, but without any markings and we should try to focus on its eastern part. I don't seem to get -- to be able to get my bearings on this map -- towards the east, yes, yes, thank you. Witness, please mark the spot where your unit was. But first of all, tell us which unit was it that you led and commanded? What were you at the time when Dragomir Milosevic was appointed commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: I was assistant commander for logistics, and I had to supply food and other amenities for the soldiers. And therefore I had to visit the lines often in order to receive suggestions and comments from the soldiers as to whether they were happy with the food and supplies, whether they had anything that they objected to and so on and so forth. And this included all of our positions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was not recorded in the transcript was that he was assistant commander. The witness was assistant commander for logistics. He was assistant commander to the battalion commander. It's still not there. Now it's okay. Show me the place of your unit where you were during the war, and make a circle around it. You mentioned Vrace.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will repeat. [Marks]. This was the line at Vrace. It went by the Jewish cemetery all the way to the bridge. That was our AOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you specifically?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: My position was at Prljavo Brdo, three kilometres away from my house that I had marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Put a circle around the area where you were.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. There you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Draw a line at which you were until the 18th of July -- no, the 16th of July, starting from Vrace.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of July, it's where the circle is. That was the area of responsibility of our forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now towards Zlatiste?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Towards Zlatiste to the right-hand side we held positions up to Zlatiste itself, and below Debelo Brdo. There was an elevation higher than Zlatiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: But Zlatiste I mentioned was the only road towards Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please stop. You started drawing the line. How far does it reach? What was the area you controlled until the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: To this line here. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Until the 16th of July, who was it that controlled Zlatiste? Mark that area as well.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. The area up to this line here was in the hands of the BH forces and we were unable to reach the road to Pale until the 16th of July. We had to go around for some 50 kilometres to reach Lukavica, towards Jahorina. It was an unpaved road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mark all that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. I started drawing the line and we had to go all the way around to Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please use another colour. Could the witness be given another pen? Please mark the positions that you assumed control of on the 16th of July. Please mark the road you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: The 16th of July. [Marks]. From this position here to here, we occupied that so that we could be able to communicate with Pale, in order to get food and to transport wounded -- the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please mark the road that was available to you after that.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. It is the road to Pale.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel and witness please not overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mr. Tapuskovic, and the witness? Please observe a pause between question and answer. The interpreter is having difficulty following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may have a moment, Your Honours, ten seconds?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Up until July, you had no other roads to Pale except for the road you had mentioned, the roundabout way?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And this posed great problems because of the wounded. It was from Vrace to Lukavica, to Tilovo [phoen] to Granice and onwards to Jahorina. We had to go there in order to reach the road to Pale and Jahorina, which is a famous ski area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The road, as you mentioned, was occupied by your forces on the 16th of July. What was its position in relation to the activities of the opposing party?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: The other side, from Zlatiste and Debelo Brdo, could reach our entire territory in depth towards Lukavica and Vrace. In addition to the fact that we were unable to use the road, they held it in their hands as of March. They put their police and troops on the road and we were unable to use it. Therefore, we had to use the roundabout way. It was a bad road and we had to use tractors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said of -- as of March. What year?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: As of the 3rd of March --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please wait for me to complete my question. Otherwise, all this will have no result. As of what day in March and of what year until when? Please wait.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: As of the 3rd of March when the barricades were set up at Zlatiste by the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic, March of what year until July of what year?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: The 3rd of March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, wait. Can't you understand that? Wait for my question to be recorded and then respond. Otherwise, the interpreters won't be able to follow. Do not hurry. Now explain.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: From the 3rd of March 1992 until the 16th of July 1992, that is the period during which their forces were there. They didn't leave the place. And they were active on those positions. On the 16th of July, we managed to liberate this stretch, which enabled us to move freely to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was the road exposed to combat activities?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: When on the 16th of July 1993, we liberated that location, and as we were moving towards the so-called Osmica and then there is a restaurant called Sumar on a plateau and to the left there is the bob piste, they from Colina Kapa were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, Your Honour. I think it is a minor point but the witness has testified about the 16th of July 1992 as being the period during which their forces were there. And then in his next answer, says the 16th of July 1993, we liberated that location. So the transcript has two different years and I just would ask for some clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Is it 1992 or 1993 that you are speaking of, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was speaking of 1992. That is the correct date. And the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
