utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned combat activities. From which directions? Mr. Visnjic, for the umpteenth time, do not start replying the very same second I stop. Wait for the transcript, have patience, do not rush. Wait for 20 or 30 seconds and then reply. Otherwise, the transcript will be incomplete. Wait. Now go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of July 1992, when we liberated the road, and when we were moving towards Pale, to the left-hand side from Osmica and the plateau I mentioned, where there was the Sumar restaurant, there was an elevation called Colina Kapa. This is where the federation forces or the forces of B and H. By using the buses.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: They opened fire at the buses that were transporting our children and women.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we had to protect the left side by making a curtain of carpets and fencing so that innocent civilians would be protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please mark the blue line with a D.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Mark the other line, going to Miljevici, I think, towards the bottom of the map, with an M.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On this map, please mark Mojmilo, and mark it to the extent possible on the map.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And approximately mark the location of Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. Debelo Brdo was here. This was our separation line and this is the Debelo Brdo elevation, which dominated, since its altitude was around 750 metres, over even Mojmilo hill, which was some 680 or 90 metres high.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Put another circle to mark Colina Kapa.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colina Kapa was somewhere here. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Zlatiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the map. Read what it says. Perhaps you can't see it. Maybe the type is too small.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is there Colina Kapa marked here?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, in that case, I cannot see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we zoom in on the western portion? Please try, since zooming in any further would make us lose the markings.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: I passed this road a thousand times. I think it was around here. Colina Kapa. I don't see it mentioned here, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please look to the right-hand side. Well, in any case, it is unimportant. Let us not waste any time.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: It is true, Your Honours, they were occupying that position. They were using the tower to fire from and there were several civilians who had been wounded on those buses, therefore we had to...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us save this map as it is, please, and tender it as a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D265, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you can now, please explain to Their Honours about the positions at Vrace where you were and the situation there, both in Dragomir Milosevic's time and throughout the conflict. I'm referring to the military aspect of the situation.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: In the area of responsibility according to the lines I drew to represent the lines of our forces, before General Milosevic's arrival in late 1994, there were assaults from Mojmilo and the Jewish cemetery and from Debelo Brdo, from the Miljacka, from the faculty of mechanical engineering, from Marin Dvor. The building where the OHR is now, it was the Union invest building before, and they kept firing and trying to pierce through those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you draw some arrows to show that? You've referred to Mojmilo, Debelo Brdo and some other positions. Please mark this with arrows.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. From this direction, the direction of Mojmilo, they attacked fiercely in depth towards Grbavica and Vrace. In late 1992 and in January and February 1993, their forces mounted one offensive after another. There was a street called Ozrenska street on our side, and when we were sending units there, it was like sending them to the east front in Hitler's time, to Russia. It was that dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please slow down, sir. Please slow down. Can you indicate this street, Ozrenska street, on the map?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. Here it is. This is Ozrenska street.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic, please don't mention any other fronts or other matters than the ones I'm asking you about. It's up to the Judges to decide on these things at the end. So please listen carefully to my questions. You said that in the courtyard of your house, there was an outpatients' clinic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, across the road from my house, there was a community centre called Aleksa Bojevic and right next to it on the plateau was a prefabricated building which was an outpatients' clinic for our citizens, all of them, Croats, Muslims and Serbs, until the conflict, and they shelled from Mojmilo. I think it was in late June 1992, when they set this prefabricated building on fire. And we were unable to save it. It burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness's testimony so far, I rise on a relevancy objection. The witness's testimony so far has seemed to me to be oriented towards establishing two points. Number 1, there was a war on and the armies fought each other. And number 2, during this war, evil things happened to people of all nationalities. Now, last time that I rose on relevancy, Mr. Tapuskovic chided me for getting up too early and not waiting until the next question, so I've waited a while but I just cannot understand the relevancy of a description of combat activities a couple of years before the indictment period to the charges that are laid in the indictment and therefore I object on the grounds of relevancy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I asked the witness what the combat activities were like throughout the war, and especially from mid-August to the end of the conflict, and the witness replied as he did. I will now focus on the relevant time exclusively, although what the witness explained refers both to the previous period and the relevant period. However, if need be, I will focus exclusively on the relevant period and I will produce some exhibits in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, please wait for my question to be recorded and don't hurry, please. This street, Ozrenska street, what happened? What did you have to do for your safety and the safety of all those in the area, especially from the 12th of August or mid-August, until the end of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have sworn to tell the truth and nothing but the truth, and I really am telling you only the truth. The area where we were, the area we defended, was under fierce fire, and to prove this, I will tell you that we had to put up boards towards Mojmilo to hide people on the street because no one could pass by without fire being opened, even on civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. We have already saved this photograph. I don't need to dwell on it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown-- is this an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we admitted the map as marked by the witness for the second time as D265, but I believe the witness made additional markings after that that haven't been tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, could I suggest that if you -- for the future when you bring maps on the screen, then wait to tender it until the end so that we don't have to admit the same picture two or three times, as that will facilitate our perception of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I understand. And that's why my examination-in-chief led to the objection by my learned friend, because I cannot show the documents I want to put to the witness as long as we have the map before us. So I am trying to deal with the map in its entirety now without having to bring it up again. Of course, I will bear this in mind, Your Honour. May this now be admitted into evidence as a Defence Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D266, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown D202? 202.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It's Defence Exhibit D202. It's on our list of exhibits, DD003355. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have just told us what this looked like. Can you explain what these photographs show?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: These photographs are very familiar to me. These are the passages we constructed closing off the right and left sides of the street, in order to reach our positions or to reach food or to take food to our civilians and fighters. And we even had to go from lamp light to lamp light, putting up canvass, carpets and all sorts of other things, because they were firing on us from Hum, from Pofalici, on Bane Surbata street, Bratstvo-Jedinstvo street, Zagrebacka street, because they could see us from up there. So by night we had to put up these things to conceal us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now have document 003335, page 29 in e-court? Look at these two pictures on the right-hand side. What does the right-hand picture show and what did the situation look like in Dragomir Milosevic's time in connection with this picture?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: I think I remember correctly, when General Milosevic arrived as commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in August, that was about the time there was a kind of lull, and this is the brotherhood and unity bridge, where there was an UNPROFOR check-point, and then the so-called Blue Road could be used by civilians to visit their children, sons, daughters, and other family members in Sarajevo, and vice versa. They could come to our area and visit their immediate family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And what is there in front of this car?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: That is a fence on Bratstvo-Jedinstvo street, brotherhood and unity street, which was there to provide protection so that one could go towards the town of Sarajevo or towards Grbavica, and what you see up above is the hill of Hum, and this is Bratstvo-Jedinstvo street. And as I said, they had an excellent view and they could use all kinds of weapons, not only infantry weapons but also mortars, 62 and 82, 60 and 82-millimetre mortars and PAMs and PATs as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be tendered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D267, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we now show document DD00335, page 15 in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you describe what we see on these photographs on the right-hand side, and is this the relevant time period as regards Dragomir Milosevic's responsibility? What is this?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, where you see these stumps of trees shows that there was fierce shooting from the BH side. You can see the state of the trees. Buildings were damaged. They were firing on a residential area. And there were many losses on our side, both civilians and soldiers were killed, but more civilians were killed because they were more careless and took greater risks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to tender these four photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D268, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Prosecution document 194? It's a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And while we are waiting for the map, can you tell us these buildings and what you have shown so far on the photographs, was all this in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of that belonged to Grbavica. There was an area in Grbavica called the so-called shopping area. That was Grbavica too. But all of that is Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we zoom in, please? A little more. Thank you. Can you tell us where on this map the positions where you were, in Dragomir Milosevic's time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: May I indicate it with this pen?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. Our positions -- this is my area of responsibility, and this bit belongs to Grbavica and Vrace and across the road is the faculty of mechanical engineering and the faculty of mathematics and natural sciences.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, where exactly were you with your unit?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. This smaller area inside here belonged to my units completely, towards Miljacka, Vraca and Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But please show us where Vrace is?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Vrace is here. That's Vrace, here in this circle. [Marks]. That's an elevation of 400 and something and this is part of Mojmilo from where they fired on our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: And on the left side was Debelo Brdo which was also an elevation of 750 and then we were in cross-fire constantly so then we had to shield our right side like I described earlier. We had to cover the streets in order to preserve the civilians and our armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when we are still on this map, while we are still looking at this map, in the summer of 1995, where did other fire at you also come from? Can you indicate that with arrows?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness's microphone please be turned on?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Earlier we said that since 1994, when General Milosevic became the corps commander, there was a truce until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, please, please, Mr. Visnjic. We will come to that. I'm asking you where did other fire come from, other than the firing from Debelo Brdo and from Mojmilo? Where did they fire at you from other places?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. From Pofalici and Hum, they fired there. And then from the Blagoja Parovic school across the street from the Genex, that's where they fired from, and they also fired from, and they also fired from -- well, that's that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where is the Blagoja Parovic school?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: The Blagoja Parovic school is located, I don't know if you know that it was to the depth of the tobacco factory, to the left there was the Genex firm and that was the Blagoja Parovic school -- street and that's where the school was. And that's where they fired from, from infantry weapons. It was practically a barracks of theirs from where their units deployed into specific positions according to the orders from their commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The place where the Blagoja Parovic school was, can you please mark that with the letters BP?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now from Vrace, did you note the positions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? If you look at this map, can you tell us what it is here that you see, these black dots? Can you please tell the Judges?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: The black dots here -- well, we were divided or separated by the Miljacka. Our positions were on this side --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please follow what I am saying. I'm talking about the right side below Debelo Brdo, these spots. Can you look at that, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right. These were their nests or positions, artillery positions, from where they fired at us from the depth. There were mortars there. Then we had to find that location, judging by the shells that they fired, in order to neutralise the firing nests from which they were jeopardising our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, can you please mark those firing nests?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Here, here and here. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, you are not following at all what I am asking you. You have indicated where Debelo Brdo is?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm asking you below Debelo Brdo do you see any firing positions? What are these black spots? That's what I'm asking you. You're marking something on the other side.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, I didn't understand you. These are the black spots from which they fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Again, just one moment, please. Do you see what is written with these large numbers there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: One -- yes, I do see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What does it say there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: 115th BB -- combat something actions. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And since you are a reserve officer, what is to the right of that number?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: These are the positions of their artillery nests from which they fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how far was that from the line of separation?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, it ranged from 200 to 300 metres from their lines. It could go as far back as 300 metres but the depth was an average of 200 metres. That's how far their mortars were situated, the 60 and the 82 millimetres and frequently, they --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, can we save this map and have it admitted as a Defence Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D269, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can the witness please be shown document DD003565? Can we please zoom in on this bottom part of the English version? Yes, the lower part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please look at the heading of the document? Who issued the document and the date, and can you please tell us who drafted the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please zoom up or scroll up? I'm talking about the bottom part of the document. No. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This bottom part, what does it say in the heading? What is the date and who signed it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: It's the 29th of June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment. Please listen to me. Can you read what it says in the heading of the document and what date is it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: All I have in the heading is that it states the commander and then above that it says we are sending -- oh, you mean to the left?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, we are not proceeding all that well. Can you please read what it states in the heading?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: "The 4th command of the 12th armoured, page number 022-11-88, Sarajevo the 29th of June 1995 at 2200 hours. I order positions -- "

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read everything?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, I am reading. "The ordering of the positions" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, you know about the rule. Read what is written. So please do that.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right. "Based according to the noticed omissions and weaknesses in the present defence system and for the purpose of overcoming the same and making better the fire system or, rather, improving the firing system, I hereby order organised firing systems at the front of the defence and organising the fire on the nearby trenches and bunkers at the depth of 50 to 100 metres wherever that is possible, also construct shields for heavy weapons. PAMMT and PM -- PMMT and PAM. That will protect positions at the front line, the forward line," I guess. I cannot read what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we please zoom in on the text a little bit?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: "At the front end of the line, and capture it. The firing positions in buildings, develop or construct bunkers or shields in front of the buildings, and capture the same and fit them in in the cited firing system."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who signed it and to whom was the document delivered to?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: To the commander, Fikret Prevljak. He is the one who signed it and who dispatched it to his superior -- or rather to his units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And which units are these?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: The 101st, the 102nd and the 105th units as well as the 115th, 150th combat brigades, the 112th and the -- the 111th and the 112th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now what you said earlier about the depth of the positions, does that coincide with what you said?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is just as I explained it earlier. Because earlier I explained that the Miljacka line, from their side, was occupied by trenches from Marin Dvor to the technical faculty all the way to the electrical utility company, and then they had these firing positions as well with heavier weapons which they fired at our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say that depth to 100 to 200 metres in relation to what?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: In relation to 100 to 200 metres into the depth of their territory behind the front lines where their forces were. So from that depth of the town, they fired at our positions from heavy weapons, and I explained that earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And was there anything even deeper into their positions? Were there any other heavy weapons there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Of course. I think that I spoke before about Pofalici and Hum, where they fired from with 120-millimetre weapon. My house was shelled on the 23rd of July 1995, and my wife was wounded in that firing, and she was treated in the Kasindol hospital. She spent about 10 days at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Time for the break. We'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we still have some time on our hands. Please bear with me, be patient, listen to my question and then respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like to ask you for a ruling for the document DD003565, that was commented on by the witness, even before he was shown the document, that this be admitted into evidence. I'd like to hear your ruling on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could you first explain to us what exactly you wish us to extract from this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness was talking about the separation line, and then he mentioned that in depth to the extent of 200 or 300 metres, that there were fortified firing positions there. He said that of his own free will. He explained where the positions were. And this is a document by a commander, Fikret Prevljak, whereby he ordered that to the front of the defence line, firing positions should be organised in such a way that cross fire can be directed from various trenches in support of the positions and heavy artillery. This confirms what the witness had stated even before he was shown the witness [as interpreted] when he said that as regards the separation line, that there was defence organised in terms of firing positions in depth, and that they had artillery at their disposal. He also said that there were similar such positions in depth, and this document, by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, by the commander of the 12th Division, which was active in the area controlled by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina absolutely confirms the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I can see that, but what I still -- excuse me, could you just let me put my question to you? What I still have difficulties in understanding is how the order from the ABiH general to his forces to develop a better system of shooting positions, how that order can possibly support your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the first thing is the one I have already stated. The second thing is that the witness already said where they were fired from. He said they were targeted from the depth, then they were firing over the heads, over their own population, over Marin Dvor and other positions occupied by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, this is firm evidence of the existence of firing positions in the depth of the territory of the ABiH, and this shows what he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And excuse me, Mr. Tapuskovic, where does this take us? I see no other probative value of this document than the fact that, yes, there was an armed conflict, yes, the ABiH was trying to improve its positions by developing a better system of locations from where fire could be addressed to the SRK, and this I think comes as no surprise to any of us. So where again, I ask, what do you want the Court to extract from this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I finish, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They fired over the heads of their population, from the very area where the incidents were. They were able to incidentally hit their own positions. They also fired incessantly from the positions that were close to the places of incident. We dispute that such incidents occurred because there was intentional firing on the part of the SRK. They fired from Hum and Zuc over the heads of entire Sarajevo and Marin Dvor. If one fires from Hum and Zuc as testified by this witness and then his wife is hit at Vrace, that shell must have flown across the entire Sarajevo and of course it can hit another couple of things along the way, sometimes intentionally so. And of course they can miscalculate the range and it can fall short of its target. This is the relevance. And I believe this document deserves all of your attention and has sufficient bearing on the decisions you are to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D270, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the witness mentioned the Blagoja Parovic school, that is also in one such location, at which such projectiles could flow over the heads of the population and he said that fire, infantry fire, was opened from the school, could we please show him document -- another document, that is the one before last out of the batch I have. It is DD002531. Can the B/C/S document be enlarged? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness please read the heading, the date? Please read out the heading, the date and the text of the order. What sort of a document is it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is a purely military document. It is an order by a commander. It came from the command of the 1st Motorised Brigade issued on the 2nd of October 1993, on the basis of a demonstrated need for better training and better performance of tasks by snipers in the 1st, 2nd and 3rd Motorised Brigade, [says the witness] I hereby order, 1, form a sniper platoon of snipers of the 1st, 2nd and 3rd motorised unit as follows:" And there is a list of names. "Item 2, I hereby appoint Muhamed Mandic," if I can read it correctly, no, it is "Medic, as commander of the sniper platoon. Item 3, the sniper platoon shall be billeted in the former Blagoja Parovic school."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this the school you mentioned and that was marked on the map?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. We touched upon the school of Blagoje Parovic. It is a large school where many units were quartered. It is actually a large barracks. In those barracks there must have been a sharp shooter's platoon that had been formed as evidenced by this order. They acted upon orders issued by their immediate commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the vicinity of the school, what sort of buildings were there and where was this infantry fire coming from, the one you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Close to the Blagoja Parovic school, there was a building of the Genex company. They had their own large distribution warehouses of consumer goods they distributed to shops, retail shops and private shops. In addition to that, there were high rises there, there was the social welfare office, the Vase Miskina metal factory premises, and the part towards Stup. From those buildings and high rises, that's where the fire was coming from, as well as from Pofalici, from the Pero Kosoric centre in Hrasno. They fired from those high rises as well as from Mojmilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I ask for this document to be admitted as a Defence Exhibit. It was received by -- from the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not why we are admitting it but we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D271, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now we are running out of time so let us try and close your examination-in-chief. Mr. Visnjic, as you said, when general came to the command post -- well, can you describe for us the period while he was commander during 1994, before he came there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: During 1994, from the moment of General Milosevic's arrival, well, before that, there were sporadic incidents and attacks by the ABiH. Upon his arrival, what followed was a calm period. As we learned later general was an exceptionally capable operational officer. He issued strict directives that were in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, that we were only to fire upon the enemy only in cases of individual provocations or an all-out attack. Otherwise, each soldier or officer would be disciplined. He did not entrust the individual officers to pass on the message to the troops but, rather, he went from one position to the next to see to it that his orders were passed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did it look like in 1994? What followed?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: In 1994, until May, there was sort of a truce, a lull, and people began feeling more safe and were going to the market. But in the summer of that year, there were provocations and individual strikes. Therefore--

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us stay in the beginning of -- the first half of the year. You said it lasted until sometime, until May. When was the truce interrupted?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: On the 26th of May, I think, by the forces of the ABiH. They attacked our lines. The intensity of attacks was particularly pronounced when they managed to pierce through --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. First and foremost, do you know when this situation picked up pace?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, it became more serious in May and June, all the way until the end of the war, concerning the Sarajevo positions and positions further on, for example in Trnovo. They attacked Trnovo on the 16th of June with a fierce attack. They managed to break through our lines. And we had to withdraw our positions by some five to six kilometres into the depth of our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember a specific incident in Vrace that remains etched in your memory?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Certainly. From Mojmilo, where our 5th company was, as well as their commander, their lines were broken through and four or five soldiers were killed. That is just below UNPROFOR positions or their base that was there. Below that base, there was a sabotage group which attacked our troops. Four men were killed and there were some wounded. Therefore, after that, we assumed position number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was it a building?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: No. It was a bunker close to the Slavisa Vajner-Cica barracks. It was their task to attack from Hum, although they could control Lukavica from Hum, but at the foot of Mojmilo there is the barracks and some 800 metres away there was another barracks called Princip Seljo, which is the barracks that housed the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did anything happen with the Investbanka building?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm very familiar with this because that building is in our zone of responsibility where the OHR is now, it was about 150 metres from Vrbanja mosque and they had to build buildings there with brick facades and on the ground floor there was the Investbanka -- bank. As they had already taken some buildings from us, they wanted to make an incursion there and they did, and the first entrance near the line, they broke through there and they got up to the third floor and they killed two or three elderly people, but then we managed to get them out of that building and hold it until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Document DD000694. Witness, look at the heading, please. What does it say underneath the heading and please read the first and the second point and tell us whether this is what you were just talking about?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: "Command of the 12th Division, Sarajevo, the 21st of July 1995, report on sabotage actions. On the 20th of July 1995, late in the evening at 200 hours I think it says here, a sabotage action was carried out in the Vrbanja Mosque which is just some metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Don't explain, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: The action was carried out by a sabotage group five -- I can't read this, it's illegible, five --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Skip over.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Something about 115th Brigade. I can't see this. And then it says: "The action was carried out against the Chetnik bunkers," is that what it says, "in Investbanka, third floor, in which Chetniks were permanently stationed. The bunker was hit with two rockets fired from an RPG 7. The action was carried out" -- I can't read this --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this what you were just explaining?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. This sabotage group broke into the Investbanka building and they got up to the third floor, on the second or third floor, there were some elderly people, they weren't all that old, 65, but they killed them and after that there was fierce fighting, because they had support from their rear and we drove them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D272, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember something that happened on this road leading from Vrace towards Pale? This is the road that was taken on the 16th of July 1992, and then when these events that happened in June and July started?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. On the 25th, I think, of June, the so-called eights [as interpreted] that I mentioned before, and a motel called Sumar, our positions were above there. I think it was number 4, there were certain units there, and between 300 and 400 hours, while our people were asleep, they liquidated them and they laid land mines there and they took up that position and, when the neighbouring bunkers heard the fighting going on, the fire was opened, and they had support from their artillery in depth in order to protect their group. And so for two or three hours we waged a battle, and they even managed to blow up that area and there was rubble blocking it but we managed to get them out of there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at document DD02?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 00325.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And look at the heading and what it says underneath, and then where it mentions our forces in 2/1, look at the sentence that begins, "In the course of the night."

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can we zoom in a bit, please? Can I begin?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: "Regular -- or rather daily combat report." But there is no heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can we scroll down a little bit, please? Scroll up, scroll up. "The command of the 12th Division, Sarajevo, 25th of June 1995. Regular-- rather daily combat report and it says, "Aggressor".

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: To where it says our forces, 2/1, look at the sentence that begins during the night. It's highlighted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours may I read it because it's been highlighted and -- or maybe the witness could look at the document on the ELMO, it will be more legible or I can read out that part of the document.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Maybe I can do my best to read it. Our forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, please, please. 2.1, the sentence that begins, "During the night" to avoid wasting time.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: "During the night, the units had no combat actions. They were preparing for offensive combat actions according to the decision of K 12 Armoured Brigade," I'm not sure what this says. It says, "05, a signal was given to start combat action at around 300 hours from automatic weapons, a serious wound was inflicted and an entry-exit wound through the right leg and the right arm, Ismet Dzaferovic of the engineers, in the course of the night," -- I can't read what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, but that's the very reason I wanted to show this. This sentence is important. Can we either put it on the ELMO or have me read it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Read it now, Witness. "In the course of the night" --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: "An explosive was laid to block the Lukavica-Trebevic-Pale road and it was activated at 5.35."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this what happened as you said when the explosive was ignited from a distance and the road destroyed?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the sabotage action they carried out. They found our men asleep and liquidated them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And were there more instances where explosives were used and ignited from a distance like this?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, it didn't happen very often but it did. I can't recall now, but this was only when their sabotage groups managed to sneak in unobserved by our forces. Then they would lay such explosives, especially at Grbavica they did that near the water works, high-rise building, but our people intervened on time -- in time because they wanted to cross the bridge, they wanted to cross the Miljacka in order to take that part of our position and that was their aim throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you very much. Can this document be tendered, please, into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Clerk.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be admitted as D273.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Sir, my name is John Docherty. I'm one of the prosecuting lawyers on this case and I have just a few questions for you today. I wanted to start with just a few questions about your background and what you did during the armed conflict. Did you testify that you were an assistant commander for logistics of a battalion?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could you tell us which battalion, please, and also who the commanding officer of the battalion was?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: My battalion was the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade, and the battalion commander was the late Radomir Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what your duties were as the assistant commander for logistics, just in a few sentences maybe tell us what you did day in, day out, what your duties were, what your responsibilities were?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: My responsibilities in logistics were mainly to supply the men on the positions with food in a timely manner, to make sure that bread was baked in the bakery which was in Tobiska street at Vrace and this bread for the troops was made at night. In the morning, the surplus was distributed to the civilians who arrived and queued up for the bread. The civilians were Muslims, Croats and Serbs. Some Muslims remained, not very many, and they took bread from that bakery after supplies had been sent to the troops. My only task was to make sure that small cars were used because large cars were too conspicuous and two of my men from the rear, one was killed and two were wounded, so even so they were targeted. And that was my task. But also, if the soldiers complained of the quality of the food, I would have to visit them in the trenches, go from trench to trench to find out what was the matter and to see why they were dissatisfied. And that's how I was familiar with all the positions on my territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. As the assistant commander for logistics, your duties did not extend, though -- you were not, for example, a member of the staff of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, were you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And were not a part of the decision-making of General Milosevic and his closest advisers, were you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: No. But we would have to carry out those orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I understand you would have to carry them out, and in fact that's what I wanted to talk with you next but my question -- the question that's before you right now is that you were not a member of the decision-make -- the senior decision-makers of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now let's turn to carrying out those orders. The Sarajevo -- do you understand what I mean if I use the term "chain of command"?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And at the time that you served in it the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had a chain of command, is that correct, in which orders given by the corps commander went to the brigade commanders, went to the battalion commanders and so on down the line until it got to the people like you who carried out orders rather than gave orders? Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, I wish to clarify this. The orders of the corps referred to the brigade commands, and battalion commands. All the brigade commands and -- all the brigade and the battalion commanders, rather, were responsible for carrying out the orders, or if they failed to carry them out they had to explain why not and why the order of the corps commander had not been carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I don't think we disagree but what I'm asking you is whether in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps it was true that more senior officers give orders to less senior officers gave orders to junior officers and so on down the line. Is that a fair description of the way things happened in the corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'm going to switch topics just now. And I'm going to ask you -- you've testified about civilians being injured and killed in your area of responsibility. But you did not testify, did you, about civilians being injured or killed on the other side of the confrontation lines, that is, in territory under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And in fact, you are aware, from various sources, are you not, that civilians in the area controlled by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina also were being killed, both by bullets and by mortar/artillery fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Most probably that's correct, but I must clarify this. The media, the BH radio we listened to, most often said how many of our soldiers were killed. They never mentioned civilians. But we never heard how many of their soldiers were killed and what losses they had. We only heard about their civilian casualties, and we always found these reports suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: But in any event, either at the time, because you were there and could see what was going on and -- or since the war, you have learned that, in fact, civilians inside the lines, in the area controlled by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina lost their lives by being shot or being shelled; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can give you a precise piece of information. On the 18th of December 1993, 20 HVO soldiers crossed the Miljacka to our side and they brought 40 Serbs with them. I was the duty officer of the battalion at the time. Every month I had to take a certain duty shift. And then they told us, I'm referring to the members of the HVO, that Celo, Caco and Puska, those were self-proclaimed defenders, prominent men, had perpetrated a genocide over the Serbian population in Sarajevo. Entire families were killed. This must be reported somewhere. And the Court must have that information. And they exaggerated the things that we did but they did those kind of things too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, I'm sure that that was a difficult day for you and I don't mean to minimise it but with all respect, sir, that's not the question that I asked you. You did not testify here today about things going on inside or in the area controlled by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you? And that's all that I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, there were several specific things that you testified to that I want to ask you some questions about. You gave testimony concerning a place called Ozrenska street. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And are you aware that in the -- a trial at this Tribunal, of General Galic, who preceded General Milosevic, that there was testimony concerning sniping of Bosnian civilians in army of Bosnia and Herzegovina areas from Sarajevo-Romanija Corps positions on Ozrenska street? Did that, Mr. Visnjic, in fact happen?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: No. I assert that Ozrenska street is below Moravska. Moravska is at a higher elevation from which our snipers could have shot, but as the crow flies, it would have been about 1.000 to 1.200 metres away and no sniper can be precise at such a distance. They could only fire at their snipers in the area of Pero Kosorica square, in Hrasno the high rise buildings from which their snipers were firing at our position. Ozrenska was the first line next to their line and there were positions at the houses there, alternating positions. One house belonging to us, another to them, and in Mojmilo they were there since 1992, and there was cross fire on us both from Debelo Brdo and Mojmilo. Debelo Brdo on the right and Mojmilo on the left looking from Vrace towards the Miljacka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, the question I was asking concerned Ozrenska street, and you may remember -- I don't want to call for the map again but you may remember making the black mark on the map. Is it not correct that you can fire into Sarajevo, into Bosnian army controlled areas from Ozrenska street? I understand you say it's a thousand to 1200 metres to some other position, but I'm talking about a straight shot into Bosnian army controlled areas of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's not true that from Ozrenska street, because these are very small houses which were quite dilapidated and already damaged by shelling, so in the cellars there were our nests and then next to them there were trenches dug into the ground. That's where our trenches were but it was not in the attic. Only from Moravska where the elevation was a bit higher, up to about 450 metres, the Moravska street elevation was possible but it didn't have the range to such a depth in Sarajevo because there were no successful snipers. I know from command meetings when they discussed that and they were obliged to come to the meeting, that it was no -- there was no point in this kind of firing because it just didn't have any effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Two things. First of all, I really have to insist on an answer to the question I put to you, which was about the range from Ozrenska street into Bosnian army controlled areas of Sarajevo. The range was not the thousand to 1200 metres you referred to a couple of answers ago, it was much shorter than that, it was a straight shot over the Miljacka river and into I believe the Marjan Dvor area of Sarajevo; isn't that correct? I understand your point about the buildings being dilapidated, the cellars, all the rest of it. I'm just asking about the range.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: The distance from Ozrenska to Marin Dvor is very far, to the right, the Pero Kosoric square or Hrasno, where the high-rise buildings were, where they acted from, that was close to us. That was possible. But as I said, that was a lower elevation and they didn't have the view to be able to do that. They could only do that from the Moravska and from that kind of plateau. That was the only way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Well, while we are talking about ranges, you had something to say about ranges in your direct testimony when you talked about fire being opened on you that had to go across the city and maybe it hit other things along the way and so forth and so on. And if we could please see Defence Exhibit 270, I'm going to be asking you some questions concerning that. But while we are waiting for the document, in your last answer or the answer before last, you mentioned that you knew it was futile to shoot from Ozrenska street because were you at staff meetings where this was discussed? Did I understand you properly? Was sniping discussed at staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: I think that it was commented upon on two occasions, when I was present at the meeting when the battalion commander would call us. I was not obliged to attend those meetings every time, only exceptionally when something was important, then I would have to be there as a logistics person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. So you would only attend the meetings exceptionally, which I take to mean rarely, and yet, even though you were attending exceptionally, sniping was discussed on two occasions when you were there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What kind of sniping? Sniping from where to where? What area was targeted by this sniping that was discussed at the staff meeting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think it's fairer to simply ask him what was discussed about sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What was discussed about sniping?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But Mr. Tapuskovic has a point. What is it, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's precisely what I wanted. What was discussed and when? What is the time period in question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The time that we discussed it in was it 1993, when their snipers were active in Grbavica and Vrace a lot and then particularly from Blagoja Parovic and those high-rise buildings, as well as two or three buildings from Vase Miskina. That's where they had an overview of our territory. Also, from Pofalici, it is the so-called Pero Kosoric square. Now it's the square of defenders of Sarajevo, Branioca Sarajevo. From those high-rise buildings, their snipers fired at us and I attended that meeting when the late Radomir Stojanovic said that our snipers must deploy so that they were at the high-rise building in Grbavica near the shopping and also from Mojmilo. So that those snipers were looking to find those other sniper nests and locate them and destroy them. This is what I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Right. So your commander, the late Radivoje Stojanovic, said that your snipers must deploy at the high-rise building in Grbavica near the shopping. Those are the tall bindings with the brick facades that you were testifying about in your direct examination, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: No, no. This is towards the Zeljo stadium. The shopping centre had two yellow high-rise buildings of about 15 to 16 storeys each, I'm not sure now, but that was that height, and they could control the Pero Kosoric square or Hrasno from there, as well as this section towards the Blagoja Parovic school and Vase Miskina where the three or four high-rise buildings were located and also from Moravska, that part of Mojmilo from where there was also sniper shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. But although I got the building, the precise building wrong, Radomir Stojanovic wanted SRK snipers in those high-rise buildings; is that right? That's what you heard?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And as far as you know, was that done?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: It was done. They belonged to our battalion so I think that was a 12-member team, not bigger than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now let's take a look at the document that is on the screen, and this is the document that led to the discussion of shooting over Bosnian positions. Now, under "order," point number 1 says, "On the front of defence, organise fire system, mutual covering," et cetera. But it does not say, and I ask you, it does not say anywhere in this document, where this -- where these positions are located; is that correct? I understand that -- you've testified about the positions but the document doesn't mention the positions, does it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: For me, it does mention that, Your Honours, because I know that in the Grbavica area, along the Miljacka, where the only thing separating us was the river, they knew exactly where our positions were, but we had fighters who had their own trenches, their own places; for example, from there they could direct their fire. Sometimes they shot at Investbanka, sometimes they attacked the water utility. There was a sabotage action. There was also a car sales plant, which I didn't mention before, that was at the very boundary of the Loris and Pero Kosoric Square. There was fierce firing there. They even tried to break through in a tunnel to reach there in order to capture that area so that they could then threaten our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, I understand that you're looking at this document and bringing to it other things that you know. But I'm looking at this document, you said that these positions are on Zuc or Hum hill and I'm asking you it doesn't say that in the document, does it? That's all, just what is in the plain text of the document.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Here, Your Honours, it said from 50 to 100 metres, and I'm going to say the following. In front -- if in front of me, let's say, there is a line, I'm speaking about the B and H army forces, you have the front lines here and then to the depth 50 to 100 metres back, how shall I put it, there is the light artillery weaponry, these are the 60s mortars and 82 mortars, and then you have the heavier weapons, 120 millimetre mortar and heavier weaponry; then they use that, those weapons, to fire at us from a depth of 500 -- 50 to 100 metres. When the guys from the hills would fire, then they would provide them with support in order to fire at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, I'm sorry, I think we are miscommunicating. You testified that the positions being discussed in this order are positions on Zuc and Hum hills, and I'm putting it to you the order doesn't say that, and that's really all I'm trying to establish and I'm ready to move on. Those words aren't in the document, are they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness, during the examination-in-chief, talked about the document in the way that he has just talked about it, but he also said that besides these positions to a depth of 100 metres, there were even further positions deeper inside from where the fire came in the way that he described. So he said that these were positions up to a depth of 100 metres and then at a greater depth, Zuc and Hum, were the places from where the fire came in the way he described. Well, in any case, the Prosecutor should show how this was stated, but in any case, what I would like to say is that during the examination-in-chief, this is the way the witness dealt with this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, you are to continue. Did you ask a question, Mr. Docherty? Is that where we are? Oh, yes, Mr. Docherty is asking to you confirm that the document does not expressly mention Zuc and Hum hills.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are not mentioned, but on the 29th of June 1995, my wife -- actually -- was wounded on the 23rd of July, by a 120 millimetre mortar shell which struck my house precisely from that direction of Pofalici and Brdo -- Humsko hill and he was -- she was wounded in one hand and on her thigh and she had a number of stitches on her wounds, and she was given a medical treatment at the Kasindol Hospital where she remained for 10 days for her medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm going to move on. I think we can all see what the document says. The weapons involved in this document under number 1, MT --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you move on, I just want to clarify. Witness, is there anything in the document in paragraph 1 that enables you to identify the positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. This document that we see here does not refer to the heavier weapons that were located further in. The lighter weaponry that I talked about, from 50 to 100 metres, refers to lighter calibre arms, 60 and 82 millimetres, which were situated immediately behind the ABiH army lines. So that's where this is mentioned. We have the PAM anti-aircraft machine-gun here with a much larger range, so it has to have a clearing and it needs a clear space in order to be able to fire. It cannot act if there are buildings in between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you saying that the reference to a depth of 50 to 100 metres assists you in identifying the positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, that was my -- actually next topic and I think you've started on it, Mr. Visnjic. The PAM there is a reference to an anti-aircraft gun. An MT, that's a machine-gun, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Machine-gun, that is right. A PM is a semi-automatic weapon and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. So no heavy artillery pieces mentioned in this document, are there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And certainly nothing called a modified air bomb mentioned in this document, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The last set of questions I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And Mr. President I think I will finish up in about certainly by ten minutes before the hour. I don't know if the Court wants to go a little longer and finish with the witness. I don't think I can finish by quarter to, but I could with an extra three or four minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, with the indulgence of the interpreters. Try to finish. That is if Mr. Tapuskovic is not going to re-examine or if he re-examines it will not be for long.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, I will have questions for re-examination, Your Honours, I need to wait until the end of the cross and then be able to give an estimate of how much time I will need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll stop in a minute. One more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm going to call for an exhibit and I'm going to ask for the witness to make one mark on it. Could we see the photograph 65 ter 2825? It's the aerial photograph of Grbavica that we've used many times before. This is not on the list, but upon hearing the witness's testimony I thought it would be useful to use; and as I say, it has been used many times before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, on the screen in front of you is a photograph. I want you to just take a minute, familiarise yourself with the scene, I'm going to ask to you make a mark on it. So just once you've got your bearings, just let me know that you're ready to go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Do I need to circle anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: The familiar buildings?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That's coming up. You testified about the Energoinvest building and about the raid on it of 21st July 1995. Is the Energoinvest building on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Please take the pen and put an X through the Energoinvest building.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Marks] This is the right flank of the building where Investbanka was, the invest bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So to be clear, the invest bank is at that X and to the left, the viewer's left?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it and we adjourn until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours this will be admitted as P786.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 26th day of June, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
